title: Daughter of God (Leviticus Rabbah 1:3)
hookLine: midrash names Pharaoh's daughter Bityah, daughter of God, for saving a child not her own
tomorrow: four kids ask about the seder. why do they get four answers?

cards: Somewhere on a family tree there is often a name nobody can place: a great-aunt from somewhere else, a surname that doesn't match. The Bible has one like that.
Deep in a list of names in Chronicles, inside the family of Judah, sits a woman called Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh. Pharaoh's daughter, in an Israelite family tree, with a Hebrew name.
Who is she, and how did she get there?

teach.b: The rabbis answer with the princess from Exodus, the one who drew the baby Moses out of the Nile. The Torah never tells us her name. But Leviticus Rabbah reads Chronicles and hears it: Bityah, bat-Yah, daughter of God.
And it gives God's reason in one balanced line. Moses was not your son, and you called him your son.
You are not My daughter, and I call you My daughter. Look at the trade. She gave a child who wasn't hers a name and a home; heaven gives her a name and a family.
The Torah's own words back her up: when the child grew, "he became her son."
Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud learns from Bityah that whoever raises someone else's child, the text counts it as if they had given birth. So the puzzle in Chronicles solves itself.

teach.h: NOT YOUR SON. NOT MY DAUGHTER.
teach.b: The daughter of the king who ordered the decree is written into Judah's family, because she opened a basket, heard a baby crying, and decided this child was hers to protect.
She doesn't switch sides by argument.
She switches by caring. Some readers see in her every grown-up who chooses a child who isn't theirs: foster parents, adoptive parents, a teacher, the neighbor who keeps an eye out.

how: Jewish law and custom honor those who raise children not born to them; the Talmud's teaching that raising an orphan is like giving birth is learned from Bityah.

games.q: a new kid on your street keeps turning up at your door at dinnertime, alone; his parents work late. by Bityah's story, what's the first move?
o: welcome him in, and let his parents know he's safe with you.
send him home; he isn't your family's responsibility.
feed him once, then let someone closer to him take over.
games.why: Bityah heard a child crying who wasn't hers and took him in. the midrash says heaven answered by calling her My daughter.

practice: Name one child who isn't yours who could use a grown-up's attention: a niece, a younger teammate, a neighbor's kid, a student.
Choose one small, appropriate thing you could do for them this week, with their parents' okay, like help with homework or a word of encouragement. Picture yourself doing it, and decide when.

wordCard.voice: Bityah: the name the midrash gives Pharaoh's daughter, heard as daughter of God, for raising a child who wasn't hers.

orig.note: Hebrew name: Bityah (Bithiah in English Bibles), heard by the midrash as daughter of God.

carryVoice: Daughter of God: what heaven calls the one who loves a child not her own. Back tomorrow.
